## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Udañcanījātaka* (Ja 106; also spelled *Udañcanijātaka*), translated as *The Water Hauler*, is a verse-narrative located in the first book (*Ekanipāta*) of the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. The Buddha is framed as recounting the story while residing at Jetavana concerning a monk tempted by a "fat girl" (*thullakumārikā*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. The commentary notes that the full background incident is related in the *Cullanāradakassapajātaka* of the Thirteenth Book (*Terasanipāta*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877].

The central verse (*gāthā*) opens with the words *Sukham vata maṁ jīvantaṁ pacamānā udañcanī*, wherein a son complains to his father of a woman who, under the pretense of being his wife, tortures him by constantly demanding provisions such as oil and salt [Fausböll 1877]. The commentary glosses the title word *udañcanī* as an instrument or vessel used for ladling water from a well (*udakam añcanti etāyā 'ti udañcanī*), functioning here as a metaphorical comparison for the woman [Fausböll 1877]. In the resolution (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the young ascetic as the discontented monk, the fat girl as the woman of the present story, and the father as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1877].

SuttaCentral registers four modern translations in four languages [SuttaCentral]. Neither SuttaCentral nor the computational analysis of DharmaNexus records any external parallels or significant Pali-internal text reuse for this story [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
